methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective single-center cohort of 195 nucleos(t)ide-analogue-naive chronic HBV patients with stored baseline serum prior to therapy (2006-2023) and longitudinal HCC surveillance during treatment. The endpoint and surveillance schedule are specified (ultrasound or dynamic CT/MRI every 3-6 months; follow-up to last visit before October 2024), and patients developing HCC within 1 year of starting therapy were excluded. Baseline lipidomics measured 158 PUFA metabolites with 76 detected and analyzed, and the study uses multiple-comparison control (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) plus time-to-event modeling (Cox). A key limitation is the low event count (19 HCC cases) relative to the number of candidate predictors, which can make multivariable estimates unstable despite selection and adjustment, and the design lacks external validation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is an individual cohort prognostic analysis linking baseline biomarkers to subsequent HCC development during antiviral therapy, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b. The clinical question is important because HCC risk persists during long-term NUC therapy, and improved baseline risk stratification could guide surveillance intensity. The manuscript reports substantial risk separation for low baseline 12-HHT (<= 3.82 ng/mL) and further stratification when combined with the routinely available FIB-4 index (cutoff 4.08), with 10-year cumulative HCC incidence of 63.1% in the high-risk group versus 1.0% in the low-risk group. While impactful if confirmed, this remains a single-center retrospective finding requiring external and prospective validation before changing clinical practice.

reporting_quality.justification: This is a prognostic biomarker study (serum metabolite profiles predicting time to HCC development), so REMARK is the most applicable reporting standard. The manuscript reports cohort definition and treatment regimen, surveillance and diagnostic criteria for HCC, laboratory assays including FIB-4 calculation, and metabolomics preprocessing (log2 transform and autoscaling) with explicit multiple-testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR). It also provides quantitative effect estimates from Cox models (e.g., low 12-HHT multivariable HR 4.28 with 95% CI 1.18-15.55) and Kaplan-Meier/log-rank analyses for cumulative incidence comparisons. Data/code sharing for the lipidomics measurements and analysis workflows is not described in the provided text, limiting reproducibility beyond the stated use of R and MetaboAnalyst.

novelty_literature.justification: The main novel finding is that low baseline 12-hydroxyheptadecatrienoic acid (12-HHT) is strongly associated with later HCC development during NUC therapy and remains significant after FDR correction among a broad PUFA-metabolite panel. The study further shows that combining 12-HHT with FIB-4 yields pronounced long-term risk stratification (10-year incidence 63.1% vs 1.0% across extreme groups), suggesting a potentially practical biomarker pair. This is more than incremental confirmation because it identifies a specific metabolite signal from a high-dimensional lipidomics screen rather than re-testing a well-established marker. The novelty is tempered by the absence of external replication and the small number of HCC events.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized with explicit sections for cohort definition, surveillance, laboratory and lipidomics assays, and statistical methods. Results provide concrete cohort characteristics (median age 46 years; 19 HCC events; median follow-up 7.4 years) and report cutoffs used for stratification (12-HHT 3.82 ng/mL; FIB-4 4.08) alongside time-horizon cumulative incidence estimates. Statistical outputs are presented with hazard ratios and confidence intervals, and the narrative ties the lipidomics screening to a single lead metabolite after FDR adjustment. Some methodological specifics (e.g., full metabolite panel details and model-selection steps) appear distributed across figures/appendices, but overall clarity is good.

key_strengths: Clinically important prognostic question: residual HCC risk during long-term NUC therapy in chronic HBV with a clearly defined surveillance/diagnosis approach.
Broad baseline lipidomics profiling (158 metabolites measured; 76 detected) with multiple-testing correction, yielding 12-HHT as a standout signal after FDR adjustment.
Time-to-event analysis with interpretable effect estimates (Cox HRs with 95% CIs) and strong absolute risk stratification when combining 12-HHT with FIB-4.
Long follow-up (median 7.4 years) enabling estimation of 5- and 10-year cumulative HCC incidence across risk strata.
key_concerns: Retrospective single-center design with only 19 HCC events creates risk of overfitting/instability in multivariable modeling and limits generalizability.
No external validation cohort is provided to confirm the 12-HHT cutoff (3.82 ng/mL) and combined risk-group performance.
Potential for confounding by fibrosis severity and other baseline clinical factors despite adjustment; event-to-predictor ratio constrains robust multivariable inference.
Data and code availability for the lipidomics measurements and analysis pipeline are not clear in the provided text, limiting reproducibility.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a promising prognostic biomarker study with striking long-term risk stratification, but the limited event count and lack of external validation mean it best fits a tier-3 venue pending major revisions focused on robustness checks and replication.
